Question::
link:{base}/activity_29-2d.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/activity_29-2d.svg[activity_29-2d]

How should this chord be labeled in the key of B♭ major?

Hint::
Remember to use the correct case for indicating the quality of the chord and to place an accidental before the Roman numeral if the root is altered.


Answer::
stem:[vii°^7]
=====


{TOP}
[[c29s4]]
=== 29.4 Mixture in major keys

In major keys, instances of mixture usually incorporate stem:[♭\hat{3}], ♭stem:[\hat{6}], or both. (stem:[♭\hat{7}] is generally avoided because its presence would subvert the important dominant function of the V and vii°.)

A lowered scale degree stem:[\hat{6}] is used to color and intensify chords built on stem:[\hat{2}] or  stem:[\hat{4}]. For example, the presence of stem:[♭\hat{6}] will make a IV chord minor (iv) as in the following excerpts:

.Example 29–7. Josepha Müllner-Gollenhofer, _Danklied_, mm. 115-123.

link:{base}/example_29-7.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_29-7.svg[example_29-7]

In mm. 120–122, a pair of stem:[V^7–I] progressions echoes the conclusion of the vocal line. The tonic is then is prolonged in m. 122 with a pair of F-minor triads. The A♭, borrowed from the parallel minor, alters the IV chords on beats two and four by making them minor. The Roman numerals are lowercase to reflect the change in chord quality.

Borrowed tones frequently originate as chromatic alterations of diatonic notes. Consider the following example:

.Example 29–8. Johann Sebastian Bach, _Weihnachtsoratorium_ (BWV 248), 33. “Ich will dich mit Fleiß bewahren,” mm. 1–3.

link:{base}/example_29-8.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_29-8.svg[example_29-8]

Here, stem:[♭\hat{6}] appears as a chromatic passing tone in the bass. It occurs with a change of harmony in the upper voices and briefly produces a minor iv chord.

Incorporating a borrowed stem:[♭\hat{6}] in a supertonic chord will turn a minor chord into a diminished chord (ii°). Seventh chords can likewise be affected by mixture. A stem:[ii^7] chord, for example, would become half-diminished (stem:[ii^{ø^7}]) with the addition of stem:[♭\hat{6}].

.Example 29–9. Maria Theresia von Paradis, Sicilienne, mm. 1–3.

link:{base}/example_29-9.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_29-9.svg[example_29-9]

As in Example 29–7 and Example 29–8, the presence of stem:[♭\hat{6}] in m. 1 makes the neighboring stem:[iv^6_4] chord minor. When an F is added in the next measure it makes a half-diminished chord out of what would have diatonically been a minor seventh.

As discussed in <<Chapter_20, Chapter 20 Fully Diminished Seventh Chords>>, this kind of borrowing happens routinely in leading-tone seventh chords. Borrowing stem:[♭\hat{6}] in a seventh chord built on scale degree stem:[\hat{7}] will change a half-diminished seventh chord to fully-diminished. The following example borrows an A♭ from C minor in m. 14:

.Example 29–10. Johann Sebastian Bach, _Das wohltemperierte Klavier I_, Prelude and Fugue 1 in C major (BWV 846), mm. 11–16.

link:{base}/example_29-10.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_29-10.svg[example_29-10]

The A♭ in m. 14 changes the quality of the leading-tone seventh chord from half- to fully-diminished.

A lowered scale degree stem:[\hat{3}] is sometimes used to produce a minor tonic where one would normally expect a major harmony:

.Example 29–11.

link:{base}/example_29-11.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_29-11.svg[example_29-11]

In this example, the concluding tonic harmony is made minor by the presence of E♭, borrowed from the parallel minor. The presence of stem:[♭\hat{3}] in a tonic harmony can have a surprising and dramatic effect! Consider the following example:

.Example 29–12. Franz Schubert, _Die Schöne Müllerin_ (D.795), 4. “Danksagung an den Bach,” mm. 16–28.

link:{base}/example_29-12.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_29-12.svg[example_29-12]

Like Example 29–1, this song uses a minor tonic to reflect a change in mood in the song’s text. Following a strong cadence in the key of G major in mm. 17–18, we encounter a minor tonic (i) in m. 22. Again, the effect is startling and intensifies the emotional tension of the moment.

Combining stem:[♭\hat{3}] and stem:[♭\hat{6}] will result in the ♭VI chord mentioned above. The ♭VI chord is one of the most commonly borrowed chords in a major key. When used in a deceptive cadence it increases the dramatic effect by thwarting to an even greater degree the listener’s expectation of tonic harmony. The following example does just this:

.Example 29–13. Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, _Don Giovanni_, Act I, Scene 5, “Madamina, il catalogo è questo,” mm. 118-127.

link:{base}/example_29-13.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_29-13.svg[example_29-13]



[[activity-29-3]]
.Activity 29–3
// [%collapsible]
=====
[[exercise-29-3]]
#_Exercise 29–3:_#

Question::
The ability to recognize and identify instances of mixture is an important skill. In what key is the following excerpt?

Frédéric Chopin, Nocturnes (Op. 32), 2. Lento, mm. 1–4.

link:{base}/activity_29-3.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/activity_29-3.svg[activity_29-3]

Hint::
What chord does the excerpt begin with?


Answer::
A♭ major

**Follow-up question**

What Roman numeral should appear at beat four in the first measure (before the B♭ in the uppermost voice)?

Hint::
Identify the root of the chord to determine the Roman numeral, then adjust the case accordingly to match the quality.


Answer::
iv
=====


{TOP}
[[c29s5]]
=== 29.5 Mixture in minor keys

<<Chapter_4, Chapter 4 Compound Meters>> introduced the concepts of the harmonic and melodic minor composites which feature raised scale degrees stem:[\hat{6}] and  stem:[\hat{7}]. These adjustments can be seen as instances of mixture, where elements of the parallel major are borrowed to suit certain harmonic and melodic contexts. Other than the ubiquitous raising of the leading tone and submediant, mixture is far less common in minor keys than it is in major keys.

Occasionally, composers will incorporate stem:[♯\hat{3}] or stem:[♯\hat{6}] to lend color to i and iv chords (i becomes I and iv becomes IV with the raising of scale degrees stem:[\hat{3}] and stem:[\hat{6}], respectively). The following example incorporates one such borrowed scale degree in m. 3:

.Example 29–14. Johann Sebastian Bach, _Bisher habt ihr nichts gebeten in meinem Namen_ (BWV 87), 7. “Muß ich sein betrübet?,” mm. 1–6.

link:{base}/example_29-14.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_29-14.svg[example_29-14]

In this example, the chord on the third beat has a B♮ in the soprano and then in the tenor. This raised third (scale degree stem:[\hat{6}]) changes the quality of the chord: what would have been minor (iv) is here major (IV). The C♯ on beat four changes the quality of the following chord to diminished (stem:[vii°^]6). Looking at the melody in the soprano part, it is easy to see that both of these alterations are a result of the melodic minor composite which, as described in <<Chapter_16, Chapter 16 Minor Scale Variants>>, is itself a type of mixture.

The following example uses a borrowed scale degree in the final chord:

.Example 29–15. Louise Farrenc, 30 Etudes (Op. 26), No. 15, mm. 71–79.

link:{base}/example_29-15.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_29-15.svg[example_29-15]

The B♯ in the final chord of this example makes the tonic major. The raised third of a tonic chord in a minor key is usually referred to as a _Picardy third_. Composers will commonly employ a Picardy third at the end of a piece in minor, coloring the conclusion with the character of a major tonic.



[[activity-29-4]]
.Activity 29–4
// [%collapsible]
=====
[[exercise-29-4]]
#_Exercise 29–4:_#

Question::
In what key is the following excerpt?

Heinrich Schütz, _Di marmo siete voi_ (SWV 17), mm. 35–36.

link:{base}/activity_29-4.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/activity_29-4.svg[activity_29-4]

Answer::
A minor

**Follow-up question**

What Roman numeral should appear under the final harmony?

Hint::
Identify the root of the chord to determine the Roman numeral, then adjust the case accordingly to match the quality.


Answer::
I

**Follow-up question**

What is the common name for this particular kind of mixture?

Answer::
Picardy third
=====


{TOP}
[[c29s6]]
=== 29.6 Mixture and basic interval progressions

Instances of mixture are often the result of adjustments made to the basic interval progressions outlined in <<Chapter_12, Chapter 12 Basic Two Voice Interval Progressions>>. In all of the harmonic progressions considered in this chapter, the voice-leading is governed by the same basic interval progressions whether mixture is present or not. In some cases, however, mixture strengthens the underlying interval progressions.

The motion from a major third to a unison is intensified by altering one of the voices to introduce semitone motion:

.Example 29–16.

{empty}a. M3–P1

link:{base}/example_29-16a.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_29-16a.svg[example_29-16a]

{empty}b. m3–P1

link:{base}/example_29-16b.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_29-16b.svg[example_29-16b]

The following example puts this into context:

.Example 29–17. Johann Sebastian Bach, “Christus, der ist mein Leben” (BWV 281), mm. 5–8.

link:{base}/example_29-17.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_29-17.svg[example_29-17]

Whereas typically the motion from a major third to a unison consists of both voices moving by whole tones, moving from a minor third to a unison reduces one voice’s movement to a semitone. The result is similar to the strong semitone/whole tone motion of a major sixth to an octave. Similarly, the motion from a major sixth to a perfect fifth is made stronger by contracting the upper-voice motion to a semitone:

.Example 29–18.

{empty}a. M6–P5

link:{base}/example_29-18a.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_29-18a.svg[example_29-18a]

{empty}a. m6–P5

link:{base}/example_29-18b.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_29-18b.svg[example_29-18b]

The following example puts this adjustment into context (Example 29–19b provides a reduction of Example 29–19a to clarify the voice-leading):

.Example 29–19. Johannes Brahms, 5 Lieder (Op. 105), 1. “Wie Melodien Zieht es mir,” mm 25–28.

a.

link:{base}/example_29-19a.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_29-19a.svg[example_29-19a]

{empty}b. reduction

link:{base}/example_29-19b.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_29-19b.svg[example_29-19b]

By lowering the F♯ to F♮, Brahms strengthens the motion to the tonic triad from m. 26 to m. 28.

While mixture often results from such voice-leading, it need not always. Sometimes, mixture is used strictly for purposes of coloration. Consider the following example:

.Example 29–20. Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, Piano Sonata No. 12 in F major (K.332), II. Adagio, mm. 1–8.

link:{base}/example_29-20.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_29-20.svg[example_29-20]

In this excerpt from the beginning of a piano sonata movement, we first hear a melody in B♭ major. In mm. 5–8 we hear the melody again. This time, however, it is presented in B♭ minor to heighten the expressiveness of the music.

{TOP}
[[c29s7]]
=== 29.7 Mixture and modulation

Most of the examples we have looked at so far are relatively small in scale. Composers borrow specific tones from the parallel key to color a chord here or there and thus dramatize the passage. But mixture can affect larger areas of music as well, particularly with regards to modulation.

Consider the following example:

.Example 29–21. Maria Theresia von Paradis, _12 Lieder auf ihrer Reise in Musik gesetzt_, 9. “Vaterlandslied,” mm. 50–60.

link:{base}/example_29-21.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_29-21.svg[example_29-21]

The third verse of the song ends unambiguously in G major (m. 52) followed by a four bar extension of the cadence in the piano. Then, after a short pause, the music shifts directly to G minor, key signature and all.

In the following example, from the same collection of songs as Example 29–25, we find a similar modulation:

.Example 29–22. Maria Theresia von Paradis, _12 Lieder auf ihrer Reise in Musik gesetzt_, 10. “Da eben seinen Lauf vollbracht,” mm. 21–28.

link:{base}/example_29-22.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_29-22.svg[example_29-22]

In m. 24 we hear a perfect authentic cadence in G major. Halfway through the same measure, though, the third of the tonic triad—somewhat hidden in an inner voice—is lowered to B♭. This inflection is initially relegated to the piano part alone. The singer does not sing scale degree stem:[\hat{3}] until the next measure. Altering the chord in this way smooths the transition between the parallel key areas.



[[activity-29-5]]
.Activity 29–5
// [%collapsible]
=====
[[exercise-29-5]]
#_Exercise 29–5:_#

Question::
The following excerpt begins in A minor but modulates in m. 24. To which key does it modulate?

Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, Piano Sonata No. 11 in A major (K.331), III. Alla Turca, iii, mm. 1–33.

link:{base}/activity_29-5.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/activity_29-5.svg[activity_29-5]

Hint::
The excerpt modulates to the parallel major.


Answer::
A major

**Follow-up question**

In the tonic key of A minor, what Roman numeral would be used to represent an A major triad?

Hint::
The root of an A major triad is the same as the root of the tonic triad in A minor.


Answer::
I
=====


In Activity 29–6 we looked at an excerpt from a piano sonata with a modulation from A minor to A major. This modulation involved a change of key signature in the middle of a bar:

.Example 29–23. Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, Piano Sonata No. 11 in A major (K.331), III. Alla Turca, iii, mm. 21–33.

link:{base}/example_29-23.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_29-23.svg[example_29-23]

As in Example 29–25, we hear a perfect authentic cadence in the original key followed by a new section of the piece in the parallel key. Once again, scale degree stem:[\hat{3}] makes the pivotal change, but here it is raised by a semitone to initiate the switch to the parallel major. Despite the mid-measure change of key signature, the listener is unaware of the new key until the downbeat of the following measure where octave C♯s are played on the downbeat. (Actually, the first C♯ we hear is in the grace note arpeggio leading to the downbeat A in the left hand.)

Modulations via mixture are not limited only to the parallel key of the global tonic. The following example in F major modulates to the key of C minor:

.Example 29–24. Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, Piano Sonata No. 12 in F major (K.332), III. Allegro assai, mm. 47–57.

link:{base}/example_29-24.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_29-24.svg[example_29-24]

In sonatas such as this one, it is quite common to encounter modulations to the key of the dominant. After a transition section ending in m. 49, we expect just that: a theme in C major. Instead, the melody beginning in m. 50 is clearly in C _minor_. The result is a move from F major to the rather distantly-related key of C minor through a mixture shift.

{TOP}
[[c29s8]]
=== 29.8 Summary

_Mixture_ consists of the borrowing of elements from the parallel key. Parallel keys differ at scale degrees stem:[\hat{3}, \hat{6}], and stem:[\hat{7}], so it is at these points that mixture will occur. In both major and minor keys, chords borrowed from the parallel key can intensify the drama of a musical texture.

Some instances of mixture can be seen as a result of strengthening the basic interval progressions governing the voice-leading of a harmonic progression. This is not always the case, however, since some cases of mixture are employed strictly for color, variation, and drama.

Mixture can have an effect on larger spans of music as well. It can initiate modulation to foreign keys via a tonicization of a borrowed chord or by moving directly to a mixture-related key area.

By incorporating chromatic pitches in this manner, composers are able to expand and enrich their options for musical expression. Though common in pieces from across the tonal repertoire, mixture is especially prevalent in music from the Romantic era. Composers in that style period were particularly concerned with the emotional impact of their music and mixture provided an effective means of heightening the level of expression.



[[Chapter_30]]
== 30. Advanced Mixture

NOTE: 简单交替 (simple mixture) 是指从平行调 (parallel key) 中借用一到多个音级，以改变和弦的性质。其他类型的交替同样会改变和弦性质，但所使用的半音变化音并非来自原调或其平行调的自然音阶。次级交替 (secondary mixture) 之中，作曲家可能通过使用此类变化音来升高或降低和弦的根音，从而改变三和弦的性质。而在双重交替 (double mixture) 中，作曲家则是对简单交替和弦进一步施加次级交替，以改变其性质。Mixture 一词也可以翻译为混织。由于罗马数字能够同时表达和弦的根音与性质，因此它们也适用于标示这三种交替类型。一如既往，罗马数字的大小写表明了和弦的性质。您应当对自然音三和弦的性质足够熟悉，以便仅通过观察罗马数字便能立即识别出是否存在半音变化。出现在罗马数字前的变音记号标示了根音的变化：前缀“♭”表示根音降低，而“♯”表示根音升高。


{TOP}
[[c30s1]]
=== 30.1 Introduction

In <<Chapter_16, Chapter 16 Minor Scale Variants>>, we discussed how minor-key compositions frequently borrow certain scale degrees from the parallel major: scale degree stem:[\hat{7}] in the case of the harmonic minor composite and scale degrees stem:[\hat{6}] and stem:[\hat{7}] in the melodic minor composite. As we saw in <<Chapter_29, Chapter 29 Mixture>>, however, the practice of sharing scale degrees between parallel keys goes far beyond these variants of the minor scale. Many tonal compositions—particularly those from the Romantic era—include passages where all three modal scale degrees (stem:[\hat{3}] in addition to stem:[\hat{6}] and stem:[\hat{7}]) move fluidly between their major and minor forms. By swapping certain notes for their parallel-key counterparts, composers are able to alter chord qualities and create some surprisingly dramatic harmonies. In this chapter we will look at other types of chromatic alterations. In these cases, though, the dramatic changes in chord quality cannot be explained as resulting from the interplay between parallel keys.

In describing these increasingly chromatic harmonies, we will push our chord-labeling system toward its limit. Roman numerals are a useful, shorthand way of naming chords, identifying their function, and showing their connection to a tonic. Although their primary purpose is to identify diatonic relationships, conventional Roman numerals may be adapted to indicate chromaticism when harmonic practice becomes more complex. Being able to recognize and use such adjustments is essential for analyzing a wide spectrum of music. This chapter will show how we expand Roman numeral conventions to deal with chromatic elements in cases of advanced mixture.

{TOP}
[[c30s2]]
=== 30.2 Roman numerals and simple mixture

由于罗马数字能够指示和弦的性质，因此它们在分析和声混合现象时特别有用。在这种情况下，三和弦通过引入平行调中的音级而改变了性质。请思考小调中建立在 第五级 和 第七级 音上的三和弦。正如在 <<Chapter_7, Chapter 7 Minor Scales>> 和 <<Chapter_29, Chapter 29 Mixture>> 中所讨论的，这两个和弦从平行大调中借用了导音。由此产生的性质差异通过罗马数字反映出来：v 变为 V，而 VII 变为 vii°。

Because Roman numerals indicate the quality of a chord, they are especially useful for analyzing instances of mixture, where triads change quality by incorporating scale degrees from the parallel key. Consider the triads built on stem:[\hat{5}] and stem:[\hat{7}] in a minor key. As discussed in <<Chapter_7, Chapter 7 Minor Scales>> and <<Chapter_29, Chapter 29 Mixture>>, these two chords borrow the leading tone from the parallel major. The resulting difference in quality is reflected in the Roman numerals: v becomes V and VII becomes vii°.

The following example shows several other examples of how Roman numerals may be used to indicate mixture:

.Example 30–1.


link:{base}/example_30-1.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_30-1.svg[example_30-1]

In a major key, the triad built on scale degree stem:[\hat{1}] is naturally major (I). When mixture is applied to the chord—lowering the third to E♭, in this case—the Roman numeral is correspondingly changed to lowercase i to indicate the minor quality. Example 30–1 also demonstrates how, through mixture, ii (minor) becomes ii°) and IV (major) becomes iv (minor).

The fourth case in Example 30–1 shows simple mixture applied to a vi chord in a major key. Here, the root of the chord is affected (A is lowered to A♭). When the root of a chord is altered, we put an accidental before the Roman numeral. The chord is labeled ♭VI: the ♭ indicates that the root—scale degree stem:[\hat{6}], as indicated by VI—has been lowered by one semitone. The case of the Roman numeral also tells us that the chord is major, and requires E♭ instead of E (with E the chord would have been augmented). The chord built on a lowered scale degree stem:[\hat{7}] (♭VII) is labeled the same way.

icon:wpexplorer[5x]
*Note:* In Example 30–1, the altered submediant chord was labeled ♭VI in C major. This same alteration in E major would require a natural sign instead of a flat in front of the note representing degree stem:[\hat{6}]:

.Example 30–2.

link:{base}/example_30-2.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_30-2.svg[example_30-2]

Notice, however, that the lowered submediant in E major is still labeled ♭VI. This brings up an important idiosyncrasy about using accidentals with Roman numerals. A lowered root is always indicated by ♭ and a raised root is always indicated by ♯, even in cases like Example 30–2 where it may not correspond with the accidentals appearing in the staff notation. (The chord built on stem:[♯\hat{7}] in minor is simply labeled vii° of ♯vii° it is so commonly used.)

You should become familiar enough with the qualities of diatonic chords that you can immediately recognize Roman numerals that indicate chromatic alterations. In the context of a major key, for instance, chords such as i and ii° instantly alert you to chromatic alterations.

{TOP}
[[c30s3]]
=== 30.3 Secondary mixture

NOTE: Secondary mixture 指借用平行调的和声概念的延伸，“次级交替” 指的是不仅从平行调（如 C 大调借用 C 小调的和弦，或反之），还从其他相关调性（例如下属调或属调的平行调）中借用和弦。这通常涉及到借用和弦的再借用，使和声色彩更加丰富和复杂。例如，在 C 大调中：普通交替 (Primary Mixture)：借用 C 小调的和弦，如 ♭VI, ♭III, ♭VII。次级交替 (Secondary Mixture)：例如，借用 F 大调的平行小调（F小调）中的和弦，如借用 F 小调的 ♭VI 和弦，即 C 大调中的 ♭II 和弦（重下属和弦）。

All of the examples of mixture presented so far have been relatively straightforward. In each case, one or two tones are borrowed from the parallel key to emphasize or intensify certain harmonies. Occasionally, however, you will encounter instances of chromatic alterations that cannot be explained in such simple terms. The following excerpt includes two chromatically-altered harmonies, one in mm. 2–3 and another in m. 7:

.Example 30–3. Franz Schubert, “Gondelfahrer” (D.808), mm. 1–13.

link:{base}/example_30-3.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_30-3.svg[example_30-3]

The A♭-major chord in m. 2 is a familiar case of simple mixture. Scale degrees stem:[\hat{3}] and stem:[\hat{6}] are borrowed from the parallel key (E♭ and A♭, respectively), changing the submediant triad from minor to major by lowering the root and fifth by a semitone each. The Roman numeral ♭VI indicates both the chord quality and the lowered root.

The sonority in m. 7, on the other hand, cannot be explained in these same terms. The major III chord is not a case of simple mixture since G♯ stem:[(♯\hat{5}]) is not drawn from the parallel minor key). In other words, an E-major triad uses pitches that do appear in C major or in C minor. This type of alteration, where a chord’s third is modified by an accidental that is _not_ borrowed from the parallel key, is sometimes referred to as _secondary mixture_. Like regular mixture, the quality of the chord in question is changed, but not through borrowing of tones from the parallel key. In Example 30–3, scale degree stem:[\hat{5}] soon reverts back to G♮ (m. 8).

The following example shows another, similar case of secondary mixture:

.Example 30–4. Franz Schubert, Piano Sonata No. 17 in D major (D.850), III. Scherzo and Trio, mm. 53–61.

link:{base}/example_30-4.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_30-4.svg[example_30-4]

The chord in mm. 57–58 cannot be explained as a case of simple mixture. As with the G♯ in Example 30–3, the quality-altering chromatic pitch D♯ (stem:[♯\hat{5}]) is not drawn from the parallel minor. This is another case of secondary mixture. The chord is again labeled with an uppercase Roman numeral III to reflect the major quality.

Despite the chromaticism, we still use Roman numerals to identify the chords described above. The following example illustrates:

.Example 30–5.

link:{base}/example_30-5.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_30-5.svg[example_30-5]

In instances of secondary mixture the quality of the chord in question is changed, but not through borrowing of tones from the parallel key. The minor quality of the diatonic ii chord becomes major (II) through secondary mixture. Likewise, iii and vi become III and VI, respectively. In each instance, the alteration is indicated by a change in the case (uppercase or lowercase) of the Roman numeral.

The following example shows both simple mixture (♭VII) and secondary mixture (II):

.Example 30–6. Franz Schubert, Allegro in A minor (D. 947), mm. 87–104.

link:{base}/example_30-6.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_30-6.svg[example_30-6]

The F-major harmony heard in mm. 93-94 is a secondary dominant tonicizing B♭. When it resolves in m. 95, however, we hear a B♭-major chord instead of the expected B♭-minor. This chord cannot be explained in terms of simple mixture since the parallel key (A♭-minor) does not include D♮. This is a case of secondary mixture: the quality of the diatonic ii chord is changed simply by raising the chordal third to the chromatic scale degree stem:[♯\hat{4}]. The G♭-major chord in m. 97 (♭VII), on the other hand, is a case of simple mixture—all three pitches (G♭, B♭, and D♭) appear in the parallel key.

Secondary mixture appears in minor keys as well:

.Example 30–7.

link:{base}/example_30-7.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_30-7.svg[example_30-7]

As shown by Example 30–7, III, VI, and VII in a minor key may be made minor through secondary mixture. In such cases, they are labeled iii, vi, and vii, respectively.

The following example includes a minor vii chord in a minor key:

.Example 30–8. Johann Sebastian Bach, _Aus tiefer Not schrei ich zu dir_ (BWV 38), 6. “Aus tiefer Not schrei ich zu dir,” mm. 11–13.

link:{base}/example_30-8.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_30-8.svg[example_30-8]

Example 30–8 shows the concluding phrase from a chorale. On the third beat of m. 12, we find a case of secondary mixture. The third of the chord has been lowered to the chromatic B♭, changing what would diatonically be a major VII chord to a minor vii chord.

Answer::
vi

**Follow-up question**

Is this a case of simple or secondary mixture?

Answer::
secondary
=====


{TOP}
[[c30s4]]
=== 30.4 Double mixture

A third type of mixture may be found in the following example, which begins in the key of C minor:

.Example 30–9. Franz Schubert, “Die Liebe hat gelogen” (D.751), mm 3–6.

link:{base}/example_30-9.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_30-9.svg[example_30-9]

At the beginning of m. 5 we find a clear-cut case of mixture: the E♮s in both the voice and the piano change the quality of the tonic triad from minor to major, and C major is then tonicized with an authentic cadence in m. 6. However, in the second half of m. 5, we find an A major triad (♯VI). With respect to C minor, all three members of that triad have been raised. This is not a case of simple mixture because C major, the parallel to C minor, does not include C♯.

This is a case of _double mixture_. Double mixture involves changing the quality of a chord derived from simple mixture. In the key of C minor, simple mixture allows for an A-minor triad ♯vi). When we encounter an A-_major_ triad ♯VI), we may think of it as being a case in which secondary mixture has been applied to a simple mixture chord, hence double mixture.

Once again, we may use Roman numerals to represent these chords. Consider the following cases of double mixture in a major key:

.Example 30–10.

link:{base}/example_30-10.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_30-10.svg[example_30-10]

In a major key, ♭III and ♭VI are both examples of simple mixture because they are derived through borrowing tones from the parallel minor. When their chord quality is changed by lowering their thirds, they become instances of double mixture. Again the Roman numeral analysis indicates the root and quality of the triad. The chord labeled ♭iii is a minor triad built on stem:[♭\hat{3}] while ♭vi is a minor triad built on stem:[♭\hat{6}].

Example 30–11 shows two examples of Roman numeral labeling for double mixture in a minor key:

.Example 30–11.

link:{base}/example_30-11.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_30-11.svg[example_30-11]

Note again that despite the natural signs altering the roots of these chords, the Roman numerals are preceded by ♯ symbols.

Now consider the following example:

.Example 30–12. Claude Debussy, “Beau Soir,” mm. 1-9.

a.

link:{base}/example_30-12a.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_30-12a.svg[example_30-12a]

{empty}b. reduction

link:{base}/example_30-12b.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_30-12b.svg[example_30-12b]

In this excerpt we find a pair of surprisingly chromatic sonorities in m. 2 and m. 4. (We hear the same chords again in m. 6 and m. 8, after the singer joins in.) Let us look at the chord in m. 4 first. If we hear the E-major opening as tonic, the chord in m. 4 may be heard as a chromatic mediant. If this was a case of simple mixture we would see and hear a G♮-major triad—G♮ (stem:[♭\hat{3}]) and D♮ (stem:[♭\hat{7}]) being borrowed from the parallel minor. Here, however, we encounter a G♮–_minor_ triad. It is as though secondary mixture was applied to a simple mixture chord and so we may think of this as an instance of double mixture.

The sonority in m. 2 (and m. 6) is complicated by the presence of pitch-class B. If the B is heard as a pedal tone—sustained through the framing E-major chords in m. 1 and m. 3—we would consider this another case of double mixture: a simple-mixture ♭VII with a secondary minor inflection. It is also possible to hear this as a neighboring sonority prolonging the tonic: the D♮ are neighbors to the Es, the F♮ are neighbors to the Es, and the As are neighbors to the Bs. (Example 30–12b demonstrates this hearing by placing the neighbor tones in parentheses.)

icon:wpexplorer[5x]
*Note:* As you can see from the explanation above, discussions involving secondary and double mixture can quickly become quite complicated. Furthermore, faced with such abundant chromaticism, you may have even found it challenging to hear E major as the tonic in Example 30–12. Given the prevalence of chromaticism in such music, one must wonder if the harmonic relationships encountered here are fundamentally different from those found in the tonal music of the high Classical era. Many listeners hear enough of a difference that they consider such music to be, in a way, _post_-tonal. Indeed, upon hearing the music, one quickly becomes aware that the tonic-dominant relationship forming the foundation of tonal harmony plays a much more peripheral role here.

It follows, then, that one should use caution when employing analytical strategies that were designed for describing a different kind of music. In recent years, music theorists have begun hearing this music on its on terms. According to this new perspective, the relationship heard between, for example, I and ♭iii may be as distinctive and foundational as any authentic cadence. It all depends on the context.

{TOP}
[[c30s5]]
=== 30.5 Other chromatic chords

A different type of chromatic chord can be seen in the following example:

.Example 30–13. Delphine Ugalde, _Seule_, mm. 1–11.

link:{base}/example_30-13.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_30-13.svg[example_30-13]

Example 30–13 begins with a pair of root-position auxiliary V chords prolonging the minor tonic. In the second half of m. 3, however, the bass leaps down to an F (scale degree stem:[\hat{4}]), harmonized in the upper voices with D♭ (stem:[♭\hat{2}]) and A stem:[\hat{6}]). This chord leads to a stem:[V^{6–5}_{4–3}] in the following measure before resolving back to the tonic. (The entire progression then repeats.) Obviously, this is not a typical case of a borrowed chord since D♭ appears in neither C major nor C minor. Furthermore, there is no such thing as a major diatonic II chord.

This particular sonority, commonly refereed to as a _Neapolitan_ chord, nonetheless occurs quite frequently. It typically appears with scale degree stem:[\hat{4}] in the bass and performs a pre-dominant function. It is a derived chord that can arise in different ways, so we label it stem:[N^6] to avoid the confusion of Roman numerals. Though not a case of mixture in the purest sense of the word, Neapolitan chords are often grouped with borrowed chords for this similarity in behavior.

Another Neapolitan chord appears in the following example:

.Example 30–14. Ludwig van Beethoven, Piano Sonata No. 14 in C♯ minor [“Moonlight”] (Op. 27, No. 2), I. Adagio sostenuto, mm. 1–5.

link:{base}/example_30-14.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_30-14.svg[example_30-14]

Following a prolonged tonic chord (with passing octave Bs in the bass), the harmony moves to VI and then to the Neapolitan—spelled F♯, A, D♮ (stem:[\hat{4}, \hat{6}, ♭\hat{2}])—before progressing to the cadential dominant.

A more detailed discussion of the Neapolitan chord can be found in <<Chapter_31, Chapter 31 The Neapolitan Chord>>.

{TOP}
[[c30s6]]
=== 30.6 Summary

_Simple mixture_ consists of borrowing one or more scale degrees from the parallel key to alter the quality of a chord. Other types of mixture also involve changing the quality of a chord, but with chromatic tones that are foreign to both the key at hand as well as its parallel. With _secondary mixture_, a composer may change the quality of a triad by raising or lowering its root with such a chromatic tone. In cases of _double mixture_, a composer changes the quality of a simple mixture chord by applying secondary mixture.

Because Roman numerals are able to express both the root and quality of a chord, they are also useful for indicating the three types of mixture. As always, the case of the Roman numerals indicates chord quality. You should become familiar enough with the qualities of diatonic triads that by simply looking at a Roman numeral you are immediately able to recognize the presence of chromatic alterations. Accidentals preceding a Roman numeral signal an altered root: a prefix ♭ indicates a lowered root while ♯ indicates a raised root.


[[Chapter_31]]
== 31. The Neapolitan Chord

NOTE: 那不勒斯和弦 (Neapolitan chord) 有时也称弗里几亚 II 级和弦 (Phrygian II)，是建立在 ♭II 级音上的大三和弦，但可以从不同角度来理解它。它可以被视作一个经过旋律性装饰的下属和弦，其五音被半音上邻音所替代——这一解释说明了为何那不勒斯和弦的低声部常出现 IV 级音，以及为何其根音（在低声部时）常被重复使用。它也可被理解为经过半音变化的 ii° 和弦，其根音被降低了半音。平行调 (parallel key) 各自的那不勒斯和弦包含相同的音高，尽管在大调中需要两个变音记号，而在小调中仅需一个。那不勒斯和弦更常见于小调，部分原因是它避免了 ii° 和弦中 II 级音 与 VI 级音 之间的三全音。作为前置属和弦 (pre-dominant)，「那不勒斯和弦」的典型功能是导向属和弦。它通常直接进行至 V 或 V⁷ 和弦，不过也常有经过副属和弦或终止式 stem:[░^6_4] 和弦插入其间。任何可用于引导 ii°⁶ 的和弦（如 i、i⁶、VI 或 iv 等）也可用于那不勒斯和弦之前。作曲家也会将其作为临时主和弦或转调到该调。无论如何，那不勒斯和弦最终总会导向某种形式的属和声。总而言之，那不勒斯和弦通常作为一种表现手法使用。其半音变化在任何语境中都十分引人注目，常被用来增强重要乐段的戏剧性张力。

{TOP}
[[c31s1]]
=== 31.1 Introduction

In the chapter on advanced mixture (<<Chapter_30, Chapter 30 Advanced Mixture>>) we introduced the Neapolitan: a type of chromatic chord that is notated as a major triad built on the lowered second scale degree (stem:[♭\hat{2}]). Another example of this sonority can be found in m. 45 of the following excerpt (the Neapolitan chord is labeled stem:[N^6]):

.Example 31–1. Maria Agata Szymanowska, 18 Danses de Différent Genre, 6. Waltz in A major, mm. 41–48.


link:{base}/example_31-1.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_31-1.svg[example_31-1]

With its major quality and lowered second scale degree, the effect of the Neapolitan is striking. As you can hear, the chord brings dramatic weight to the ensuing cadence and intensifies the passage in a way that a diatonic pre-dominant chord cannot.

In this chapter, we will examine the origins and structure of the Neapolitan chord. Depending on the context, the Neapolitan can be derived in several ways—hence the label stem:[N^6] instead of a Roman numeral. With an understanding of how these derivations work, we will investigate how the Neapolitan functions in various conditions. We will also discuss how the Neapolitan behaves over larger spans when it is tonicized or used in a modulation.

{TOP}
[[c31s2]]
=== 31.2 Origin and structure

The Neapolitan chord may be thought of as a voice-leading sonority derived from an embellished subdominant triad:

.Example 31–2.

{empty}a. iv chord in C minor

link:{base}/example_31-2a.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_31-2a.svg[example_31-2a]

{empty}b. iv chord with chromatic upper neighbor tone

link:{base}/example_31-2b.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_31-2b.svg[example_31-2b]

{empty}c. assimilation of chromatic upper neighbor tone

link:{base}/example_31-2c.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_31-2c.svg[example_31-2c]

Example 31–2a shows a iv chord in C minor. Example 31–2b shows the same iv with its fifth decorated by a chromatic upper neighbor tone (D♭). In Example 31–2c, the root and third of the iv chord are sustained under the upper neighbor. With the chromatic neighbor assimilated into the chord, a new consonant triad is formed (D♭-major). It is labeled stem:[N^6]. Note that the superscript stem:[^6] here does not indicate an inversion, since scale degree stem:[\hat{4}] is still the foundation. Rather, it is a bass figure and indicates that a sixth appears above the lowest note.

This understanding of the Neapolitan accounts for its tendency to appear as what looks like a first-inversion triad, with the chordal third doubled. If the Neapolitan is considered a derivation of iv, it is in fact the root (the bass) that is being doubled—the norm for root-position triads! Consider the following example:

.Example 31–3. Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, Piano Trio in E major (K.542), III. Allegro, mm. 137–144.

link:{base}/example_31-3.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_31-3.svg[example_31-3]

Here, a Neapolitan chord appears in m. 142. The F♯ in the bass allows for a smooth, stepwise ascent to scale degree stem:[\hat{5}] (m. 143). As you can see in the melody, the D♮ is a chromatic upper neighbor to C♯. The following example replaces the D♮ with a diatonic C♯ in m. 142:

.Example 31–4. Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, Piano Trio in E major (K.542), III. Allegro, mm. 137–144, with diatonic iv instead of stem:[N^6].

link:{base}/example_31-4.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_31-4.svg[example_31-4]

With C♯ sustained through m. 142, the resultant sonority would be a iv chord in root position. Like a root-position iv chord, the Neapolitan usually appears with scale degree stem:[\hat{4}] in the bass (see also Example 31–1).

The following excerpt consists of two phrases, the second of which has a Neapolitan chord:

.Example 31–5. Alice Charbonnet, Danse des sorcières, mm. 13–28.

link:{base}/example_31-5.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_31-5.svg[example_31-5]

The two phrases in Example 31–5 (mm. 13–20 and mm. 21–28) are nearly identical. The primary difference may be found by comparing m. 17 to m. 25. In m. 17 we find a stem:[iv^6] chord acting as functional pre-dominant leading to the cadence that ends the phrase. The notes in m. 25 are exactly the same except the fifth of the iv chord (A) has been replaced with its chromatic upper neighbor (B♭). (The bass note has been changed too—from F to D—allowing for smooth passing motion between the stem:[i^6] in m. 24 and the cadential stem:[░^6_4] in m. 26.) The parallelism between these two measures shows the strong connection between stem:[iv^6] and stem:[N^6].

.Activity 31–1

image:{base}/activity_31-1d.svg[activity_31-1d]

Hint::

D must be replaced with E♭.
=====


The Neapolitan chord can also be thought of as a chromatic alteration of the diatonic ii chord. Example 31–6 shows how Neapolitan chords can be derived this way in both major (a) and minor (b) keys:

.Example 31–6.

{empty}a. derivation of stem:[N^6] from stem:[ii^6] in major

link:{base}/example_31-6a.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_31-6a.svg[example_31-6a]

{empty}b. derivation of stem:[N^6] from stem:[ii°^6] in minor

link:{base}/example_31-6b.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_31-6b.svg[example_31-6b]

In both cases, the resultant chord consists of the same three tones. Note that in major keys, however, the Neapolitan requires two accidentals: stem:[♭\hat{2}] (D♭ in this case) and stem:[♭\hat{6}] (A♭). Though not rare in major keys, Neapolitan chords are more commonly encountered in minor. The major quality of the Neapolitan differs dramatically from the diminished diatonic ii° and provides an effective means of stabilizing it by eliminating the tritone between its root and fifth (minor scale degrees stem:[\hat{2}] and stem:[\hat{6}]).

icon:wpexplorer[5x]
*Note:* The name of the Neapolitan chord links it to the so-called “Neapolitan school”—a group of composers active in and around Naples, Italy in the 18^th^ century. However, there is little historical justification for this as the chord was certainly used earlier and by composers as far away as England.

You might also see the chord labeled “Phrygian II,” referring to Phrygian scale which differs from major and minor scales by beginning with a minor second between its first and second degrees. (This name should not be taken to imply that the music has shifted to Phrygian, but rather that the chord has some similarity in sound with the scale.) Other texts use the abbreviation stem:[♭II^6], since the chord can also be thought of as a major triad built on stem:[♭\hat{2}]. For our purposes, we label the chord stem:[N^6] and refer to it as the Neapolitan.

The following example shows a Neapolitan derived from an altered ii chord (Example 31–7b provides a reduction of Example 31–7a):

.Example 31–7. Ludwig van Beethoven, Symphony No. 7 (Op. 92), I. Poco sostenuto – Vivace, mm. 364–370.

a.

link:{base}/example_31-7a.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_31-7a.svg[example_31-7a]

{empty}b. reduction

link:{base}/example_31-7b.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_31-7b.svg[example_31-7b]

The stem:[ii^6_5] chord in m. 366 leads to a Neapolitan in m. 368. Following the voice leading in the upper parts, we can see that the B♭ of the Neapolitan comes directly from the root of the stem:[ii^6_5] chord (B♮). Though it has the same construction as a Neapolitan derived by embellishing iv, this Neapolitan is clearly an altered ii chord. Nonetheless, the chord is once again supported by scale degree stem:[\hat{4}] in the bass.

=====

'''''

image:{base}/activity_31-2b.svg[activity_31-2b]

Hint::

'''''

link:{base}/activity_31-2c.mp3[{play}]

Hint::

'''''

[[exercise-31-2d]]
#_Exercise 31–2d:_#

Question::
Adjust the necessary pitch or pitches in the following stem:[ii^6] chord to create a Neapolitan in F major:

link:{base}/activity_31-2d.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/activity_31-2d.svg[activity_31-2d]

Hint::
Remember, in a major key, the root and fifth of the stem:[ii^6] chord need to be lowered.


Answer::
G must be replaced with G♭ and D with D♭.
=====


To summarize, the Neapolitan can be thought of in two ways. In the first, the fifth of a subdominant triad is replaced by its chromatic upper neighbor. The resultant sonority is a major triad: stem:[N^6]. (Remember that in this case the superscript stem:[░^6] is a bass figure indicating that a sixth appears above the lowest note. It does not indicate that the chord is in an inverted position.) In the second conception, the Neapolitan is derived by chromatically lowering the root of a diatonic ii°. (In major keys, scale degree stem:[\hat{6}] must also be lowered.) These dual derivations are why we label the Neapolitan generically, using stem:[N^6] instead of a Roman numeral.

Of the two, the latter is more common today since the usual notation of the Neapolitan more readily resembles a stem:[♭II^6] chord than a iv chord with an altered fifth. Nonetheless, it is important for analysis that you be able to conceive of the Neapolitan in both ways. Consider the following example:

.Example 31–8. Frédéric Chopin, Nocturnes (Op. 55), 1. Andante in F minor, mm. 5–8.

link:{base}/example_31-8.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_31-8.svg[example_31-8]

In this excerpt from a Chopin Nocturne, we find a Neapolitan following a root position III chord. In this case, the Neapolitan must be considered an embellished iv. To view this Neapolitan as stem:[♭II^6] would be counterintuitive and would contradict the norms of harmonic root movement. The Neapolitan is a passing chord from III to V. In other words, the progression stem:[III–iv^{♭6}–V^6_4] makes much more sense than stem:[III–♭II^6–V^6_4].

Now consider the following example (Example 31–9b provides a reduction):

.Example 31–9. Franz Schubert, String Quartet No. 12 (D.703), mm. 7–19.

a.

link:{base}/example_31-9a.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_31-9a.svg[example_31-9a]

{empty}b. reduction

link:{base}/example_31-9b.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_31-9b.svg[example_31-9b]

This passage consists of two parallel phrases. The first of these (mm. 7–13) includes a Neapolitan chord as an extension of iv through an auxiliary passing stem:[░^6_4] chord: stem:[i–iv^6–(i^6_4)–N^6–V–i]. A parallel phrase follows in mm. 15–19. This time, however, the Neapolitan has been replaced by stem:[ii°^6]. By presenting these two chords—stem:[N^6] with its stem:[♭\hat{2}] and then stem:[ii°^6] with its diatonic stem:[\hat{2}]—within parallel phrases in close proximity, the composer highlights the contrast between different versions of the ii chord. As you can see, it is important that you be able to conceptualize the Neapolitan in both ways.

{TOP}
[[c31s3]]
=== 31.3 Other positions of the Neapolitan

Although the Neapolitan usually appears with scale degree stem:[\hat{4}] in the bass, other positions are possible. The following example shows one such instance:

.Example 31–10. Frédéric Chopin, Prelude No. 20 in C minor (Op. 28), mm. 11–13.

link:{base}/example_31-10.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_31-10.svg[example_31-10]

On the second beat of m. 12, we find a Neapolitan chord with the chromatic pitch (stem:[♭\hat{2}]) in the bass. (Note that instead of stem:[N^6], the chord is labeled stem:[N^5_3] indicating the third and fifth that appear above the bass.) This voicing brings out the chord’s startling, dramatic effect by dramatizing the tritone in the low register when the bass, reinforced by octaves, leaps from D♭ to G. Cases of stem:[♭\hat{2}] in the bass supporting a Neapolitan are far less frequent than those with stem:[\hat{4}] in the bass. This voicing of the Neapolitan is rare because composers usually tend to avoid accentuating tritones in this manner.

{TOP}
[[c31s4]]
=== 31.4 Function, voice-leading, and context

Regardless of how you think of the Neapolitan chord— as a neighbor-note embellishment of iv (IV in major) or as a chromatic root-alteration of ii° in major)—it retains the pre-dominant function of its origin. In other words, the Neapolitan chord routinely signals and leads to some form of dominant. It frequently moves directly to the dominant (V or stem:[V^7]), as in the following excerpt:

.Example 31–11. Franz Schubert, _Die Schöne Müllerin_ (D.795), 19. “Der Müller und der Bach,” mm. 1–10.

link:{base}/example_31-11.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_31-11.svg[example_31-11]

Here the Neapolitan chord appears in m. 8 after two full measures of tonic harmony. It then moves directly to a V chord in the following measure which in turn resolves to i at the end of the phrase.

Note that in Example 31–11, stem:[♭\hat{2}] (A♭) is emphasized as the highest note in the piano part and leaps down a diminished third to the leading tone (F♯). While this diminished melodic interval would typically be avoided, composers tend to highlight it in the case of the Neapolitan by putting it in the soprano. Like the leading tone, stem:[♭\hat{2}] is only a semitone away from the tonic and as such has a strong tendency to resolve to  stem:[\hat{1}]. However, because the Neapolitan is a pre-dominant chord, the dominant chord further delays the resolution to  stem:[\hat{1}]. The heightened harmonic tension brought on by this delay makes the Neapolitan chord a potent dramatic tool.



[[activity-31-4]]
.Activity 31–4
// [%collapsible]
=====
When analyzing Neapolitan chords, it is essential that you be able to recognize the altered pitch or pitches and trace the voice-leading from one chord to the next.

'''''

[[exercise-31-4]]
#_Exercise 31–4:_#

Question::
Identify the Neapolitan chord in the following excerpt:

.Ludwig van Beethoven, Piano Sonata No. 14 in C♯ minor [“Moonlight”] (Op. 27, No. 2), I. Adagio sostenuto, mm. 1–5.

link:{base}/activity_31-4.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/activity_31-4.svg[activity_31-4]

Answer::
The Neapolitan is in the second half of m. 3.

**Follow-up question**

Does the stem:[♭\hat{2}] of the Neapolitan move to the leading tone or diatonic stem:[\hat{2}]?

Answer::
stem:[♭\hat{2}] leaps down a diminished third to the leading tone.
=====


When stem:[N^6] moves to V, the upper voices usually move in contrary motion to the bass. The bass note (scale degree stem:[\hat{4}]) almost invariably steps up to stem:[\hat{5}] while the upper voices move down to the nearest chord members:

.Example 31–12.

link:{base}/example_31-12.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_31-12.svg[example_31-12]

In SATB settings such as the one in Example 31–12, the bass note stem:[\hat{4}]) is usually doubled. This is due in part to the remaining chord members having a strong tendency to move down: (♭)stem:[\hat{6}] steps down to stem:[\hat{5}] and, as described above, stem:[♭\hat{2}] leaps down a third to the leading tone.

When stem:[N^6] moves to stem:[V^7], the doubled note stem:[\hat{4}]) may be suspended in one of the upper voice:

.Example 31–13.

link:{base}/example_31-13.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_31-13.svg[example_31-13]

Problems arise when the notes of the Neapolitan do not move in contrary motion to the bass:

.Example 31–14.

link:{base}/example_31-14.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_31-14.svg[example_31-14]

In Example 31–14, the motion from stem:[♭\hat{2}] to stem:[♮\hat{2}] in the soprano line creates an awkward chromatic contour. The lowered second scale degree will sometimes lead to the diatonic second scale degree, but this tends to be restricted to inner voices since the upward motion contradicts the tendency for stem:[♭\hat{2}] to resolve down to  stem:[\hat{1}].

=====


In other cases, the Neapolitan does not move directly to V. Instead, an intervening chord may delay the dominant. Consider the following examples:

.Example 31–15. Franz Schubert, “Erlkönig” (D.328), mm. 140–148.

link:{base}/example_31-15.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_31-15.svg[example_31-15]

.Example 31–16. Johann Sebastian Bach, _Ach Gott, vom Himmel sieh darein_ (BWV 2), 6. “Das wollst du, Gott, bewahren rein,” mm. 1–4.

link:{base}/example_31-16.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_31-16.svg[example_31-16]

The Neapolitan chord in Example 31–15—itself embellished with an auxiliary sonority in m. 144—leads to an applied stem:[vii°^7/V] in m. 147 before moving to the cadential V chord. The same technique appears in Example 31–16. Here, an unprepared Neapolitan is used to begin a phrase following a half cadence. A stem:[vii°^7/V] delays the dominant, which arrives one beat later.

icon:wpexplorer[5x]
*Note:* Despite the key signature with just one flat, Example 31–16 is in G minor. In Johann Sebastian Bach’s time, it was common for minor key signatures to be written with one less accidental, owing to remnants of earlier notational conventions.

Example 31–17 shows a similar situation in which the Neapolitan leads to a cadential  stem:[░^6_4] chord:

.Example 31–17. Felix Mendelssohn, _Lieder ohne Worte_ (Op. 102), 4. Un poco agitato, ma andante, mm. 3–7.

link:{base}/example_31-17.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_31-17.svg[example_31-17]

Note that in this example, the VI chord preceding the Neapolitan can also be interpreted as an applied dominant (continuing the falling fifth pattern from the previous measures). If the first half of m. 5 is regarded as V/N, then the Neapolitan in this case has loosened its ties to the original iv chord with 5–6 motion over the bass stem:[\hat{4}]). The Neapolitan has taken on a harmonic identify of its own, by virtue of the preceding applied dominant. We will return to this topic momentarily in the section on tonicizing the Neapolitan.

Whether the Neapolitan proceeds to an applied diminished seventh chord (as in Examples 31–15 and 31–16) or to a cadential  stem:[░^6_4] (Example 31–17), stem:[♭\hat{2}] may at first appear to resolve melodically directly to  stem:[\hat{1}]. But that stem:[\hat{1}] is a false resolution and is not heard as a true arrival since it is not supported by consonance with the bass. It acts instead as a passing tone—a dissonant diminished fifth or perfect fourth above the bass—on the way to the leading tone. The melodic resolution of stem:[♭\hat{2}] occurs with the arrival of the leading tone over V, and the harmonic resolution occurs when that V resolves to I.



[[activity-31-6]]
.Activity 31–6
// [%collapsible]
=====
As a pre-dominant chord, the Neapolitan leads to dominant harmony. Sometimes, however, another pre-dominant chord intervenes. Recognizing this delay in the arrival of the dominant is an important part of analysis.

'''''

[[exercise-31-6]]
#_Exercise 31–6:_#

Question::
Identify the first appearance of the Neapolitan chord in the following excerpt. (Note that despite the key signature, this passage is in the key of A major.):

Joseph Haydn, Keyboard Sonata in D major (Hob.XVI:37), I. Allegro con brio, mm. 28–35.

link:{base}/activity_31-6.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/activity_31-6.svg[activity_31-6]

Hint::
A good way to identify Neapolitan chords is to look for the expected chromatic alterations. In a major key, these are the lowered scale degrees stem:[\hat{2}] and  stem:[\hat{6}].


Answer::
The Neapolitan chord first appears on the downbeat of m. 30.

**Follow-up question**

In this case, the Neapolitan does not move directly to the dominant. In what measure does the root-position dominant seventh arrive?

Hint::
Look for a chord that measure whose pitches are that of a dominant seventh chord.


Answer::
The true dominant harmony arrives in m. 34.

**Follow-up question**

What two other pre-dominant chords intervene between the Neapolitan and the true dominant harmony?

Answer::
The Neapolitan leads to a stem:[vii°^7/V] in m. 32 and then a cadential stem:[░^6_4] in m. 33 before getting to the dominant in m. 34.
=====


The same chords that are typically used to approach stem:[ii(^°)^6] are also used to approach the Neapolitan. Example 31–10 and Example 31–17 show Neapolitan chords following VI. Example 31–15 has a Neapolitan following iv—the A♭s beginning in m. 143 act initially as chromatic upper neighbors to the fifth of the iv chord. Example 31–7 has a Neapolitan following stem:[ii^6_5] and Example 31–1 and Example 31–3 approach the Neapolitan with tonic triads.

{TOP}
[[c31s5]]
=== 31.5 Tonicizing the Neapolitan

Composers frequently tonicize the Neapolitan. The structure of the minor scale makes this particularly convenient since the diatonic VI chord is equivalent to the dominant of the Neapolitan. In other words, the progression stem:[VI–N^6] can sound like stem:[V/N–N^6](a tonicization of the Neapolitan) since the root motion is the same as V–I.

Consider the following example:

.Example 31–18. Maria Agata Szymanowska, 6 Minuets, No. 1 in A minor, mm. 1–16.

link:{base}/example_31-18.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_31-18.svg[example_31-18]

In Example 31-18, after a pair of authentic cadences in (m. 4 and m. 9), we hear a deceptive cadence in m. 12. This F-major chord is heard initially as VI in A minor. On the other hand, the root of this chord (F) lies a perfect fifth above—or a perfect fourth below—the root of the Neapolitan that follows. The F-major chord may, in other words, also be heard as V/N setting up the chromatic B♭ in m. 13.

Composers will occasionally expand this sort of tonicization by modulating to the key of the Neapolitan for extended passages. Tonicizations of—and modulations to—the Neapolitan in a minor key are possible because, as pointed out earlier, chromatically altering stem:[\hat{2}] to become stem:[♭\hat{2}] stabilizes the unstable, diminished ii° into a major triad, ♭II.

A similar scenario appears in the following example:

.Example 31–19. Frédéric Chopin, Mazurkas (Op. 7), 2. Vivo, ma non troppo in A minor, mm. 9–16.

link:{base}/example_31-19.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_31-19.svg[example_31-19]

The Neapolitan is tonicized here with an applied dominant seventh chord in m. 13. This applied chord is derived by adding a minor seventh above the root of the preceding VI chord (E♭).

The following excerpt provides another example of a tonicized Neapolitan

.Example 31–20. Johann Sebastian Bach, Organ Sonata No.4 in E minor (BWV 528), II. Andante, mm. 1–3.

link:{base}/example_31-20.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_31-20.svg[example_31-20]

This passage includes a Neapolitan chord in the opening phrase. On the second beat of m. 2, we see an E in the bass with G and C♮ in the upper voice—a typical example of a Neapolitan chord. Preceding this, we find a VI chord consisting of G in the bass with B and D in the upper voice. This chord can also be interpreted as an applied dominant to the Neapolitan. (It is labeled V/N in Example 31–20.) As an applied dominant, this tonicization of the Neapolitan continues a falling fifth progression begun in the previous measure. By moving to the Neapolitan, Bach avoids the tritone root motion that would have resulted from VI to a diatonic ii°. (For more information on applied chords, see <<Chapter_27, Chapter 27 Applied Chords>>.)

No matter what the length—single chords, tonicizations, modulations—appearances of the Neapolitan soon lead to the dominant. Emphasizing the Neapolitan by making it sound temporarily like a tonic dramatizes the arrival of the dominant.

{TOP}
[[c31s6]]
=== 31.6 Summary

The _Neapolitan chord_ (sometimes referred to as _Phrygian II_) is notated as a major triad built on stem:[♭\hat{2}], but can be conceptualized in different ways. It can be thought of as a melodically embellished subdominant chord whose fifth has been replaced by its chromatic upper neighbor—an explanation that accounts for the tendency of the Neapolitan to appear with stem:[\hat{4}] in the bass, and for the bass, as root, to be doubled. It can also be thought of as a chromatically altered stem:[ii(^°)] chord, in which the root has been lowered by a semitone.

The respective Neapolitan chords of parallel keys contain the same tones, though two accidentals are required in major as opposed to the single accidental required in minor. Neapolitan chords appear more frequently in minor keys, in part because they avoid the tritone between stem:[\hat{2}] and stem:[\hat{6}] in the ii°.

As a pre-dominant chord, the Neapolitan’s typical function is to lead to the dominant. It often does this directly—moving to V or stem:[V^7] without delay—though frequently an applied chord or cadential stem:[░^6_4] intervenes. Any chord used to approach stem:[ii(^°)^6]  can also precede a Neapolitan: i, stem:[i^6], VI, or iv among others. Composers also tonicize it or modulate to that key. In any case, the Neapolitan eventually leads to some form of dominant harmony.

All in all, the Neapolitan is generally used as an expressive device. The chromatic alteration is striking in any context and is often used to heighten the dramatic tension of important passages.



[[Chapter_32]]
== 32. Augmented Sixth Sonorities

NOTE: 增六度和弦 (Augmented sixth sonorities) 构成以 stem:[♭\hat{6}] 或者小调的 stem:[\hat{6}] 到 stem:[♯\hat{4}] 增六度不协和音为特征。如同双导音 (dual leading tones) 以楔形方式向外扩张，并通过半音进行解决到 stem:[\hat{5}] 级音。因此，增六度和弦起到半音化的前置属和弦功能，与同样涉及半音变化的那不勒斯和弦归为同一类别。stem:[♯\hat{4}] 级音的存在将它们与副属和声联系起来，但它们不应被理解为使属和弦临时主音化。由于其独特而引人注目的性质，它们常被用来标示重要的结构终止式。 由 stem:[♭\hat{6}] 级音 和 stem:[♯\hat{4}] 级音 构成的音程是这些和弦的决定性特征，但它们通常与其他音符的三种组合之一同时出现：意大利增六和弦在低音上方包含一个大三度（即 stem:[\hat{1}] 级音，通常被重复）；法国增六和弦在低音上方包含一个大三度和一个增四度（即 stem:[\hat{1}] 和 stem:[\hat{2}] 级音）；而德国增六和弦（这三种类型中最常见的一种）在低音上方包含一个大三度和一个纯五度（即 stem:[\hat{1}] 级音 和 stem:[♭\hat{3}] 级音，在小调中为 stem:[\hat{3}] 级音），并具有最丰富的织体。 增六度和弦也可用于延伸进行和转调。由于它们与属和弦 V 紧密相连，可用于有效地标示转调目标调的新属和弦。此外，德国增六和弦与属七和弦之间的等音关系 (enharmonic equivalence)，使得德国增六和弦成为转调到远关系调（其主音相距半音）的便捷手段。


{TOP}
[[c32s1]]
=== 32.1 Introduction

The example below shows an excerpt from a string quartet. Notice the intriguing chromatic sonority in m. 5:

.Example 32–1. Ludwig van Beethoven, String Quartet No 2 (Op. 18, No. 2), III. Scherzo. Allegro, mm 1–8.


link:{base}/example_32-1.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_32-1.svg[example_32-1]

Following a stem:[IV^6] chord in m. 4, the outer voices expand in contrary motion to form an augmented sixth (A♭ in the bass with F♯ in the treble). As the sonority moves to V in the following measure, we see that the outer voices both resolve outward by semitone to G. Just as a leading tone lies a half step away from the tonic, A♭ and F♯ both lie a half step away from G. We may think of them as dual leading tones to scale degree stem:[\hat{5}], since each approaches its destination with half-step motion. The only difference between these notes and a typical leading tone is that in this case one of the notes (A♭) moves in the opposite direction.

Of course, this type of sonority could never occur diatonically. No two diatonic pitches will produce an augmented sixth. Nevertheless, chromatic sonorities containing an augmented sixth appear quite frequently. As you will see in this chapter, there are several types of chromatic sonorities characterized by the presence of an augmented sixth, appropriately referred to as _augmented sixth sonorities_. As seen in Example 32–1, augmented sixth sonorities characteristically function as pre-dominant chords and usually lead to dominant harmony. Like other chromatic sonorities, augmented sixths can have a striking effect that composers exploit in order to heighten dramatic tension or highlight important structural moments.

After discussing the general structure and derivation of augmented sixth sonorities, we will look at the three common types and their function in tonal music. We will then examine several complex uses of this type of sonority.

{TOP}
[[c32s2]]
=== 32.2 Structure and derivation

Augmented sixth sonorities are derived by chromatically altering a common basic interval progression. (See <<Chapter_12, Chapter 12 Basic Two Voice Interval Progressions>> for more on how basic interval progressions lie at the base of all voice-leading.)

.Example 32–2.

{empty}a. M6–P8

link:{base}/example_32-2a.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_32-2a.svg[example_32-2a]

{empty}b. A6–P8

link:{base}/example_32-2b.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_32-2b.svg[example_32-2b]

{empty}c. A6–P8 with inner voice

link:{base}/example_32-2c.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_32-2c.svg[example_32-2c]

Example 32–2a shows the familiar basic interval progression of a major sixth expanding to an octave, as it might appear in the common progression stem:[iv^6–V] (in this case, in A minor). Here, the lower voice descends to stem:[\hat{5}] by semitone while the upper voice ascends by whole tone to the same scale degree. Raising scale degree stem:[\hat{4}], as in Example 32–2b, will produce an augmented sixth. Now both voices are only a semitone away from their respective destinations. Example 32–2c fills out the sonority with an inner voice. Augmented sixth sonorities invariably include scale degree stem:[\hat{1}]—a major third above the bass—which moves to the leading tone in the ensuing dominant harmony.

As Example 32–2 demonstrates, augmented sixth sonorities may arise from chromatic alterations of pre-dominant chords. They retain that function and most commonly lead to the dominant. In Example 32–2, for instance, we see that raising the root of a stem:[iv^6] chord creates an augmented sixth with the bass. The tritone between stem:[\hat{1}] and stem:[♯\hat{4}] is another characteristic dissonance of all augmented sixth sonorities. Rather than undermine the function of the iv chord, the chromatic pitch in fact intensifies the pre-dominant function. The dual contrary-motion voice-leading by semitone to stem:[\hat{5}], combined with the dual contrary-motion resolution of the tritone between stem:[\hat{1}] and stem:[♯\hat{4}] (also by semitone), drives augmented sixth sonorities powerfully toward the dominant.

Augmented sixth sonorities also occur in major contexts. There, they require an extra accidental to lower scale degree stem:[\hat{6}] so that it is a semitone away from  stem:[\hat{5}]. Example 32–3 reproduces Example 32–2c in A major. As you can see, the augmented sixth requires an accidental to lower the F♯ (stem:[\hat{6}] in A major) to F♮, a semitone above stem:[\hat{5}]:

.Example 32–3.

link:{base}/example_32-3.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_32-3.svg[example_32-3]

(For the sake of consistency, we will here use stem:[♭\hat{6}] to generically refer to the pitch a semitone above stem:[\hat{5}], even though minor keys require no additional accidental and sometimes a natural sign is used in major keys.)

=====

Raised scale degree stem:[\hat{4}] (stem:[♯\hat{4}]) appears in other chromatic harmonies as well, most notably in applied chords. (See <<Chapter_27, Chapter 27 Applied Chords>> for more on applied chords.) In stem:[V^7/V], for example, stem:[♯\hat{4}] acts as a temporary leading tone to  stem:[\hat{5}]. But stem:[♯\hat{4}] never appears in conjunction with stem:[♭\hat{6}] in an applied chord to V, nor should you interpret the presence of stem:[♯\hat{4}] in an augmented sixth as tonicizing V. Augmented sixth sonorities, as chromatic pre-dominants, emphasize the arrival of the dominant but do not tonicize it.

Augmented sixth sonorities usually appear with stem:[♭\hat{6}] in the bass, often with stem:[♯\hat{4}] in the treble to emphasize the chromatic expansion to the octave. Other positions are possible, but occur less frequently. That said, augmented sixth sonorities with other scale degrees in the bass should not be considered “inversions” since stem:[♭\hat{6}] is not a “root” in the same sense as the root of a triad or seventh chord.

{TOP}
[[c32s3]]
=== 32.3 Types of augmented sixth sonorities

There are three varieties of augmented sixth sonorities, each containing a different “filling,” so to speak, within the framework of the augmented sixth. These varieties are identified with geographical names—Italian, French, and German—none of which is historically or geographically justifiable. The names are widely used, however, and we will use them here since they permit easy identification.

It is important to remember that augmented sixths are embellishing sonorities, not structural chords. They cannot be constructed purely from diatonic notes and therefore cannot be goals of modulation. Like auxiliary sonorities—another type of chord arising from voice-leading procedures—augmented sixths are a combination of simultaneous melodic embellishments. The different types listed below occur with enough frequency to merit discussion, but their differences simply arise from combinations of nonharmonic tones. Though the inner-voice filling may vary, it is the augmented sixth between stem:[♭\hat{6}] and stem:[♯\hat{4}] that gives the sonority its aural signature and requires the most attention.

{TOP}
[[c32s4]]
=== 32.4 Italian augmented sixths

The simplest type of augmented sixth sonority is the Italian. In addition to stem:[♯\hat{4}] and stem:[♭\hat{6}] forming the augmented sixth framework, this sonority contains one other pitch a diatonic major third above the bass (scale degree stem:[\hat{1}]), as seen in Example 32–2c. The Italian augmented sixth sonority is sometimes referred to as the augmented 6/3. This does not imply that the chord is a triad in first inversion. Rather, it simply indicates the presence of a third and a sixth above the bass.

icon:wpexplorer[5x]
*Note:* You may occasionally see augmented sixths indicated by a bass figure six with a slash through it:

.Example 32–4.

link:{base}/example_32-4.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_32-4.svg[example_32-4]

This is a common figured bass convention. The slash indicates that the sixth above the bass should be raised by a semitone: in this case requiring D♯ instead of D♮.

Other music theory texts include a superscript “{plus}” sign to emphasize that the sixth is augmented: It^{plus}^6. In this chapter we will use abbreviations of the geographic nicknames combined with bass figures. In other words, “stem:[It^6]” is short for “Italian augmented sixth.”

The following example shows an Italian augmented sixth sonority in a musical context:

.Example 32–5. Felix Mendelssohn, Lieder ohne Worte (Op. 30), 4. Agitato e con fuoco, mm. 52–60.

link:{base}/example_32-5.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_32-5.svg[example_32-5]

In this excerpt, we find an arpeggiation of a VI chord in mm. 56–58. We expect this pattern to continue in m. 59, but encounter there an E♯ where the arpeggiation of G-major harmony in mm. 56–58 points toward a G. The substitution of E♯ (scale degree stem:[♯\hat{4}]) for G creates a dissonant augmented sixth with the bass G (scale degree stem:[\hat{6}]). The sonority is filled in with a B in the tenor (a major third above the bass) and all three voices resolve, as expected, to a dominant in m. 60: stem:[♭\hat{6}] and stem:[♯\hat{4}] move to stem:[\hat{5}] while the tritone formed by stem:[\hat{1}] and stem:[♯\hat{4}] resolves outward to a minor sixth. The harmonic effect, though brief, is striking and emphasizes the arrival of the dominant in a way that a diatonic chord cannot.

Now consider the following example:

.Example 32–6. Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, Piano Sonata No.12 in F major (K.332), I. Allegro, mm. 116–126.

link:{base}/example_32-6.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_32-6.svg[example_32-6]

Here, the Italian sixth appears directly after a root-position tonic. The inner-voice D in the tonic remains stationary while the outer voices expand to form the augmented sixth, B♭–G♯. All three voices move as expected to the V chord at the beginning of m. 123.

Italian sixth chords in textures with four or more voices always double the third above the bass (scale degree stem:[\hat{1}]). Note that the inner voices move in contrary motion to one another, and also in contrary motion to their registral companions:

.Example 32–7.

link:{base}/example_32-7.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_32-7.svg[example_32-7]

As you can see in Example 32–7, the doubled scale degree stem:[\hat{1}] moves to both the leading tone and to scale degree stem:[\hat{2}] in the ensuing V chord. Scale degrees stem:[♯\hat{4}] and stem:[♭\hat{6}] are never doubled since doing so would lead to parallel octaves as a result of their strong tendency to resolve to  stem:[\hat{5}].

The following excerpt shows an Italian sixth in four voices (note that, despite the key signature, this passage begins in G minor):

.Example 32–8. Johann Sebastian Bach, “Ich hab mein Sach Gott heimgestellt” (BWV 351), mm. 1–2.

link:{base}/example_32-8.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_32-8.svg[example_32-8]

On the second beat of the first full measure, we find an Italian sixth: stem:[♭\hat{6}] in the bass, stem:[\hat{1}] in the soprano and tenor, and stem:[♯\hat{4}] as a chromatic lower neighbor to the D from the preceding i chord. Again, all four voices resolve as expected to the pitches of the V chord.

Now consider the following example:

.Example 32–9. Louise Farrenc, _20 Etudes de moyenne Difficulté pour Piano_ (Op. 42), No. 17, mm. 1–8.

link:{base}/example_32-9.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_32-9.svg[example_32-9]

In this excerpt, an Italian sixth appears at the end of m. 7, just after a tonicized subdominant chord. Notice the similarity between the stem:[iv^6] and the stem:[It^6]. The two chords are nearly identical, the only difference being that the root of the stem:[iv^6] is (D) replaced by a chromatic passing tone (D♯). In this case, the Italian sixth does not progress directly to a V chord. Instead, it moves to another strong dominant function chord: a cadential stem:[░^6_4]. The resolution of the augmented interval, however, remains the same—F and D♯ each move a half-step in contrary motion to octave stem:[\hat{5}]s.

#_Exercise 32–4:_#

Maria Agata Szymanowska, 6 Marches for Piano, No. 5 in B♭ major, Trio, mm. 1–8.

**Follow-up question**

Does the Italian sixth move directly to V? Or is there some intervening sonority?

Hint::
Does m. 7 begin with a root-position dominant?


Answer::

Maria Agata Szymanowska, 6 Marches for Piano, No. 5 in B♭ major, Trio, mm. 1–8.

link:{base}/activity_32-4_answer.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/activity_32-4_answer.svg[activity_32-4_answer]

{TOP}
[[c32s5]]
=== 32.5 French augmented sixths

The Italian sixth is relatively thin in texture, containing only three unique pitch classes. The French sixth, by contrast, adds an augmented fourth above the bass (scale degree stem:[\hat{2}]) and produces significantly more dissonance among the voices. It is sometimes referred to as an augmented 4/3 chord, though this is not to imply that it is a seventh chord in second inversion. Example 32–10 illustrates:

.Example 32–10.

link:{base}/example_32-10.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_32-10.svg[example_32-10]

We can see the voice-leading already familiar to us from the Italian sixth: stem:[♯\hat{4}] and stem:[♭\hat{6}] resolve outward by semitone to stem:[\hat{5}], and the third above the bass (scale degree stem:[\hat{1}]) steps down to the leading tone. Instead of doubling stem:[\hat{1}], as in the Italian sixth, we’ve added a fourth voice: B (stem:[\hat{2}]). Since scale degree stem:[\hat{2}] is also the fifth of the dominant chord, it is commonly held when the French sixth resolves to V.

The incorporation of stem:[\hat{2}] into the French sixth leads to yet another tritone, this time with the bass. The presence of two tritones stem:[\hat{1}–♯\hat{4}] and stem:[♭\hat{6}–\hat{2}]) gives the French sixth its characteristically piercing sound. The added dissonance adds an even greater urgency to the sonority, further activating its tendency to resolve to V.

Observe the voice leading in the following example:

.Example 32–11. Ludwig van Beethoven, Piano Sonata No. 8 [“Pathétique”] (Op. 13), III. Rondo. Allegro, mm. 44–47.

link:{base}/example_32-11.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_32-11.svg[example_32-11]

In the second half of m. 46 we find a clear example of a French augmented sixth. As you can see, the outer voices come about as chromatic passing tones: stem:[♭\hat{6}] (C♭) steps down to stem:[\hat{5}] (B♭) and stem:[♯\hat{4}] (A♮) steps up to  stem:[\hat{5}]. Scale degree stem:[\hat{1}] is held over from the preceding stem:[IV^6] chord while stem:[\hat{2}], completing the two-tritone make-up of the French sixth, is introduced in anticipation of the V chord.

Example 32–12 shows another instance of a French augmented sixth:

.Example 32–12. Ludwig van Beethoven, Piano Sonata No. 4 (Op. 7), II. Largo con gran espressione, mm. 72–74.

link:{base}/example_32-12.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/example_32-12.svg[example_32-12]

Here, the dissonant augmented sixth is introduced gradually. An applied stem:[vii°^6/V] chord follows an auxiliary passing stem:[░^6_4] chord in m. 73, introducing the temporary leading tone F♯ stem:[(♯\hat{4})]. (Were the F left natural, the harmony would have followed the common stem:[IV–(I^6_4)–IV^6] progression.) The bass then steps down chromatically to A♭, forming an augmented sixth with stem:[♯\hat{4}]. The tonic pitch is sustained throughout, and in the highest voice we find stem:[\hat{2}], completing the French sixth sonority. In this case, the augmented sixth sonority does not resolve directly to the dominant. Instead it introduces a cadential stem:[░^6_4] chord like we saw in Example 32–9.

**Note:**The doubling of stem:[♭\hat{6}] in Example 32–12 appears to lead to parallel octaves as the French sixth moves to the cadential stem:[░^6_4]. This is the result of doubling the bass line at the octave. True parallel octaves occur between two independent voices. These octaves simply arise from doubling, which is used here to create a thicker texture.

Write a four-voiced French augmented sixth sonority in A♭ major.

Hint::
In a major key, a French augmented sixth will have stem:[♭\hat{6}] in the bass with stem:[♯\hat{4}, \hat{1}], and stem:[\hat{2}] in the upper voices.

Answer::
link:{base}/activity_32-5d_answer1.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/activity_32-5d_answer1.svg[activity_32-5d_answer1]

(Answers may vary, provided F♭ is in the bass and B♭, A♭, and D♮ appear in the upper voices.)

**Follow-up question**

Resolve this French sixth to a dominant triad using proper voice-leading.

Hint::
Remember, the voices forming the augmented sixth will expand outward to octave stem:[\hat{5}]s, while stem:[\hat{1}] moves to the leading tone and stem:[\hat{2}] is sustained.


Answer::
link:{base}/activity_32-5d_answer2.mp3[{play}]
image:{base}/activity_32-5d_answer2.svg[activity_32-5d_answer2]

(Answers may vary, provided F♭ moves to E♭, A♭ moves to G, D♮ moves to E♭, and B♭ is sustained.)
